--- title: "Linear model" subtitle: "Fit voxel-wise first-level models with the typed fmrimod API." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- ## A Typed Spec and a Dataset The canonical first-level path is `fmri_lm(spec, dataset)`. The spec is a typed value built from `hrf(...)`; the dataset binds data to timing and events. No string formula, no hand-built design matrix. ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod.spec import hrf from fmrimod.contrast import condition events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": np.arange(6, 198, 8.0), "condition": ["face", "scene", "tool"] * 8, "duration": 2.0, }) spec = hrf("condition", basis="spmg1") ``` ::: We use simulated data with a **known** `face − scene` effect of `2.5` in five of ten voxels, so a correct model must return ≈ `2.5` there and ≈ `0` elsewhere — that known answer is what makes the fit checkable. `dataset_with_effect` is a tutorial helper that builds the data with the effect placed on the `condition("face", ...)` column, the same object the contrast below tests. ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from fmrimod.simulate.demo import dataset_with_effect sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=220, TR=1.0) dataset = dataset_with_effect( spec, events, on=condition("face", term="condition"), effect=2.5, sampling_frame=sampling, seed=5, ) ``` ::: ## Fit the First-Level Model `fmri_lm()` compiles the spec, builds the full event-plus-baseline design, and returns an inspectable typed result. ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit = fm.fmri_lm(spec, dataset) fit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` FmriLm( n_coefficients=4, n_voxels=10, residual_df=216.0, config=FmriLmConfig(OLS), contrasts=[], ) ``` ::: ::: The realized design is inspectable from the fit — you never built it by hand, but you can still read every column. ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame( fit.betas, index=list(fit.model.design_matrix(run=0).columns), ).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## A Typed Contrast The hypothesis names conditions, not column indices. `fit.contrast(...)` returns a `ContrastResult`, and the estimate comes back at ≈ `2.5` — the value we injected. A model that fit cleanly but applied the contrast to the wrong columns would return a different number here. ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} face_vs_scene = fit.contrast( condition("face", term="condition") - condition("scene", term="condition"), name="face_vs_scene", ) pd.DataFrame({ "estimate": face_vs_scene.estimate.round(3), "t": face_vs_scene.stat.round(2), "p": face_vs_scene.p_value.round(4), }) # voxels 0–4 recover ≈ 2.5; voxels 5–9 are null ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

It skips the spec, the column provenance, and the contrast machinery, so reach for it only when you specifically want a bare-matrix cross-check — for example, to confirm the high-level fit against textbook OLS, as below. For actual analyses, stay on `fmri_lm`. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = np.asarray(fit.model.design_matrix_array(run=0)) matrix_fit = fm.fmri_ols_fit(dataset.get_all_data(), X) # The low-level solver and the typed fit return identical betas. np.allclose(matrix_fit["beta"], fit.betas) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ## Next - [The golden path](golden-path.qmd) — the whole workflow into group, with a parity check - [Contrasts](contrasts.qmd) - [Sketched and AR-aware models](sketched-ar-models.qmd)
